payload.set_intro:
Historical source (real document)
These documents are real historical sources (excerpts are cut verbatim from the repository text; [...] marks an omission). Document 4 is an image shown below the documents.

Document 1 (primary source)
Man and Nature; or, Physical Geography as Modified by Human Action (excerpt)
George P. Marsh, American diplomat and scholar, 1864 (New York: Scribner). Project Gutenberg eBook #37957. Reuse: public domain in the United States (published before 1929). excerpted (1 segment); whitespace normalized; no wording changed.
Context: George P. Marsh was an American diplomat who had served in the Ottoman Empire; when he published this book in 1864 he was the United States minister to Italy.

"The earth is fast becoming an unfit home for its noblest inhabitant, and another era of equal human crime and human improvidence, and of like duration with that through which traces of that crime and that improvidence extend, would reduce it to such a condition of impoverished productiveness, of shattered surface, of climatic excess, as to threaten the depravation, barbarism, and perhaps even extinction of the species."

———

Document 2 (primary source)
Our National Parks, ch. 1 (excerpt on the forest reserves)
John Muir, Scottish-American naturalist, 1901 (Boston: Houghton Mifflin). Project Gutenberg eBook #60929. Reuse: public domain in the United States (published before 1929). excerpted (1 segment); whitespace normalized; no wording changed.
Context: John Muir was a Scottish-born American naturalist; he published this book in 1901.

"The forty million acres of these reserves are in the main unspoiled as yet, though sadly wasted and threatened on their more open margins by the axe and fire of the lumberman and prospector, and by hoofed locusts, which, like the winged ones, devour every leaf within reach, while the shepherds and owners set fires with the intention of making a blade of grass grow in the place of every tree, but with the result of killing both the grass and the trees."

———

Document 3 (primary source)
Worlds in the Making: The Evolution of the Universe (excerpt on carbonic acid and temperature)
Svante Arrhenius, Swedish chemist (English translation by H. Borns), 1908 (English edition; Swedish original 1906). Project Gutenberg eBook #69022. Reuse: public domain in the United States (published before 1929). excerpted (1 segment); whitespace normalized; no wording changed.
Context: Svante Arrhenius was a Swedish chemist; this book was published in English in 1908.

"With the help of these data I have calculated that if the atmosphere were deprived of all its carbonic acid—of which it contains only 0.03 per cent. by volume—the temperature of the earth’s surface would fall by about 21°. This lowering of the temperature would diminish the amount of water vapor in the atmosphere, and would cause a further almost equally strong fall of temperature. The examples, so far as they go, demonstrate that comparatively unimportant variations in the composition of the air have a very great influence. If the quantity of carbonic acid in the air should sink to one-half its present percentage, the temperature would fall by about 4°; a diminution to one-quarter would reduce the temperature by 8°. On the other hand, any doubling of the percentage of carbon dioxide in the air would raise the temperature of the earth’s surface by 4°; and if the carbon dioxide were increased fourfold, the temperature would rise by 8°."

———

Document 4 (photograph)
Dust bowl, Texas Panhandle (photograph made for the Resettlement Administration; held in the Library of Congress FSA/OWI Collection)
Arthur Rothstein, photographer for the Resettlement Administration (the agency was folded into the Farm Security Administration in 1937), 1936 (March). Wikimedia Commons (file page records the source institution and public-domain tag). Reuse: public domain (U.S. government work). unmodified except Wikimedia Commons' scaled JPEG rendering of the file (upload.wikimedia.org thumbnail).
Context: A photographer working for a U.S. government agency took this photograph in the Texas Panhandle in March 1936.

The image for this source is shown below. Select the image to open it full size.

———

Document 5 (table)
Atmospheric carbon dioxide at Mauna Loa Observatory, annual mean (ppm), selected years 1960-2020
NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory (data from 1958-1974 obtained by C. David Keeling, Scripps Institution of Oceanography), Annual means; data file retrieved October 19, 2026. NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory. Reuse: public domain (U.S. government data; credit NOAA GML and Scripps as requested). seven rows copied from the 'mean' column of the annual-mean file (CO2 mole fraction in dry air, ppm); no values changed or recomputed.
Context: The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration measures carbon dioxide in the air at an observatory on a Hawaiian volcano; this table shows annual averages for seven years.

| Year | Annual mean CO2 (ppm) |
| --- | --- |
| 1960 | 316.91 |
| 1970 | 325.68 |
| 1980 | 338.76 |
| 1990 | 354.45 |
| 2000 | 369.71 |
| 2010 | 390.10 |
| 2020 | 414.21 |

———

Document 6 (secondary source)
Soviet Union: A Country Study (excerpt on environmental degradation)
Raymond E. Zickel, ed., Federal Research Division, Library of Congress, 1991. Library of Congress, Federal Research Division (Country Studies; full text via Internet Archive OCR). Reuse: public domain (U.S. government work, 17 U.S.C. 105). excerpted (1 segment); whitespace normalized; OCR line-break hyphenation rejoined; running page headers/numbers removed; no wording changed.
Context: This reference book was written for the U.S. government in 1991, before the Soviet Union ended.

"As a consequence of this neglect, two of the twentieth century's worst man-made environmental disasters struck the Soviet Union: the Chernobyl' nuclear power plant accident, the consequence of an insufficient regard for safety to obtain increased energy; and the loss of huge amounts of water from the Aral Sea. Although the death toll from the Chernobyl' accident in 1986 was initially low, millions of people continued to live on radioactive land and raise and consume contaminated food. In addition to the human costs, cleaning up and repairing the after-effects of the accident, which continued to leak radioactive gases in 1991, were estimated to cost hundreds of billions of rubles (see Glossary) by the year 2000. The other major environmental disaster was the near destruction of the Aral Sea, whose main sources of water were diverted to irrigate arid land for the purpose of raising cotton and other crops beginning in 1960. Subsequently, the Aral Sea's coast receded sixty kilometers, in places, from its former location. Other environmental problems included the severe pollution of rivers, lakes, and the air resulting from the direct discharge of pollutants, particularly in the European part of the Soviet Union."

———

Document 7 (secondary source)
Brazil: A Country Study (excerpt on deforestation and development)
Rex A. Hudson, ed., Federal Research Division, Library of Congress, 1998. Library of Congress, Federal Research Division (Country Studies; full text via Internet Archive OCR). Reuse: public domain (U.S. government work, 17 U.S.C. 105). excerpted (1 segment); whitespace normalized; OCR line-break hyphenation rejoined; no wording changed.
Context: This reference book was written for the U.S. government; the passage describes Brazil in the early 1990s.

"The topics of rapid deforestation and extensive burning of the Amazon rain forest and environmental pollution received unprecedented international attention in the late 1980s and early 1990s. Water and air pollution had also become a serious problem for Brazil. Sao Paulo State's Tiete is so polluted that in 1992 the state was forced to launch a US$2.6 billion program to revive it. In June 1992, Rio de Janeiro hosted the United Nations (UN) Conference on the Environment and Development (Eco-92). However, the Brazilian government's attention to the problems of deforestation and pollution waned following Eco-92, despite the creation in late 1993 of the Ministry of Environment and the Amazon Region. In the mid-1990s, discussion of public policies intended to promote sustainable development (see Glossary) remained intense."

parts.prompt:
From the middle of the nineteenth century onward, industrialization, commercial agriculture, the extraction of resources and state-directed development changed landscapes, waterways and the atmosphere in many parts of the world. Writers, scientists, governments and international bodies offered different explanations of how far human activity was reshaping nature and what should be done about it. The seven documents run from George P. Marsh's 1864 book to carbon dioxide measurements taken through 2020.

Evaluate the extent to which understandings of the relationship between human activity and the natural environment changed from the mid-nineteenth century to the early twenty-first century.

In your response you should do the following:
- Respond to the prompt with a historically defensible thesis or claim that establishes a line of reasoning.
- Describe a broader historical context relevant to the prompt.
- Support an argument in response to the prompt using at least four documents.
- Use at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence (beyond that found in the documents) relevant to an argument about the prompt.
- For at least two documents, explain how or why the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience is relevant to an argument.
- Use evidence to corroborate, qualify, or modify an argument that addresses the prompt.
parts.model_answer:
Between the mid-1800s and the early 2000s, understandings of how humans affect nature changed a lot in scale and method, but less in basic idea than it might seem. Early writers like Marsh and Muir already believed human carelessness could ruin the land, and they judged this by looking at forests and soil. By the late twentieth century, scientists measured damage to the whole atmosphere with instruments, and governments and international meetings treated the environment as a global political issue. Still, one thing stayed the same: governments kept putting economic development ahead of protecting nature, even when they knew the risks.

This change happened because of how the world economy grew. The Industrial Revolution spread from Britain to the United States, Germany and Japan in the 1800s, and factories, railroads and steamships ran on coal. Imperial and commercial expansion also pushed farming and mining into new areas, from the American West to colonies in Africa and Asia. In the twentieth century, oil and planned economies like the Soviet Union's sped up resource use even more. So more people were seeing environmental damage, and it was getting bigger.

In the nineteenth century, concern was mostly based on what people could see. Marsh warned in 1864 that the earth was "fast becoming an unfit home" and that human "improvidence" could even lead to the "extinction of the species" (Doc 1). This shows that even early on, some thinkers saw the danger as covering the whole planet and not just one place. Marsh's point of view matters here. He was a diplomat who had served in the Ottoman Empire and Italy, places where land had been farmed and cleared for thousands of years, so he could compare old worn-out Mediterranean landscapes with the young United States and warn Americans that their land could end up like that. Muir in 1901 described logging, fires and sheep, which he called "hoofed locusts," destroying the forest reserves (Doc 2). Like Marsh he judged damage by looking at it, and he wanted it protected. This fits with the founding of Yellowstone as the first national park in 1872, which showed the U.S. government starting to set land aside.

The understanding started to shift toward the atmosphere with science. Arrhenius calculated that doubling carbon dioxide would raise the earth's temperature by about 4 degrees (Doc 3). However, his excerpt does not blame industry or ask for any policy. It is a scientific calculation, which shows that knowing about a connection did not automatically mean people saw it as a problem yet. Meanwhile, damage on the ground got worse. The 1936 photograph of a huge dust storm in the Texas Panhandle (Doc 4) shows how plowing up the Great Plains destroyed the soil. The purpose of this photo matters, because it was taken for the Resettlement Administration, a New Deal agency. The government wanted to show the public how bad the crisis was so people would support its programs to help farmers and change how land was used. This shows that by the 1930s the government itself saw human farming practices as the cause of disaster.

After 1950 the biggest change was measurement. The Mauna Loa data shows carbon dioxide rising every decade from about 317 ppm in 1960 to 414 ppm in 2020 (Doc 5). This turned Arrhenius's theory into something people could track year by year, and it gave a planetary view of human impact.

But continuity remained in how governments acted. The Soviet Union diverted rivers to grow cotton, and the Aral Sea shrank badly, and Chernobyl in 1986 came from "insufficient regard for safety" to get energy (Doc 6). This was written by the U.S. government in 1991 during the end of the Cold War, so it may have focused on Soviet failures to make communism look bad, though the disasters really did happen. Brazil also hosted Eco-92, but attention "waned" afterward (Doc 7). So even though understanding became global and scientific, the conflict between development and nature that Muir described continued into the 1990s.

rubric_rows.criterion: A claim that evaluates how much understandings changed, for example arguing that concern moved from damaged forests, soils and regions toward a planetary and atmospheric view while the conflict between economic development and conservation continued. It must set up a line of reasoning, not just say that things changed.

Places the argument within broader developments, such as industrialization and the use of fossil fuels, imperial and commercial expansion of agriculture and resource extraction, the Great Depression and the New Deal, Cold War planned economies, or decolonization and globalization of environmental diplomacy after 1970.

Uses what the documents actually say or show: Marsh's warning about a planet made unfit by human improvidence, Muir on grazing, logging and fire in the forest reserves, Arrhenius's calculations linking carbon dioxide to temperature, the 1936 dust storm photograph, rising Mauna Loa readings, Chernobyl and the Aral Sea, and Brazil's deforestation and Eco-92.

At least one specific piece of evidence not in the documents, such as the founding of Yellowstone in 1872, the Soil Conservation Service in 1935, Rachel Carson's Silent Spring in 1962, the Montreal Protocol of 1987, the creation of the IPCC in 1988 or the Kyoto Protocol of 1997, used to support the argument.

Explains how point of view, purpose, historical situation or audience shapes at least two documents, for example Marsh's diplomatic posts in the Ottoman Empire and Italy, the U.S. government origin of the 1936 photograph, or the U.S. government authorship of the 1991 Soviet study written before the Soviet Union ended.

Shows a complex understanding, for instance by weighing change against continuity, separating scientific understanding from political action, or using documents that qualify the main claim, such as the Soviet state causing damage or Brazil's attention to the issue fading after Eco-92.

payload.reference_text:
Scoring guide (ALTON reference — not official AP scoring). This question is worth 7 points.
Thesis/claim (0-1): A claim that evaluates how much understandings changed, for example arguing that concern moved from damaged forests, soils and regions toward a planetary and atmospheric view while the conflict between economic development and conservation continued. It must set up a line of reasoning, not just say that things changed.
   - 1: Gives a defensible claim about the extent of change in understandings of human impact on nature, with a line of reasoning, in the introduction or conclusion.
   - 0: No claim, a restatement of the prompt, or a claim that does not evaluate the extent of change.
Contextualization (0-1): Places the argument within broader developments, such as industrialization and the use of fossil fuels, imperial and commercial expansion of agriculture and resource extraction, the Great Depression and the New Deal, Cold War planned economies, or decolonization and globalization of environmental diplomacy after 1970.
   - 1: Describes a broader historical development before, during or after the period that connects directly to the argument.
   - 0: No relevant context, or only a passing phrase.
Evidence from the documents (0-2): Uses what the documents actually say or show: Marsh's warning about a planet made unfit by human improvidence, Muir on grazing, logging and fire in the forest reserves, Arrhenius's calculations linking carbon dioxide to temperature, the 1936 dust storm photograph, rising Mauna Loa readings, Chernobyl and the Aral Sea, and Brazil's deforestation and Eco-92.
   - 2: Uses at least four documents to support an argument about the extent of change.
   - 1: Accurately describes the content of at least three documents and relates them to the topic.
   - 0: Uses fewer than three documents accurately, or only quotes or lists them.
Evidence beyond the documents (0-1): At least one specific piece of evidence not in the documents, such as the founding of Yellowstone in 1872, the Soil Conservation Service in 1935, Rachel Carson's Silent Spring in 1962, the Montreal Protocol of 1987, the creation of the IPCC in 1988 or the Kyoto Protocol of 1997, used to support the argument.
   - 1: Uses at least one specific, accurate piece of outside evidence to support the argument.
   - 0: No outside evidence, or evidence only mentioned in passing or not connected to the argument.
Sourcing (point of view, purpose, situation, audience) (0-1): Explains how point of view, purpose, historical situation or audience shapes at least two documents, for example Marsh's diplomatic posts in the Ottoman Empire and Italy, the U.S. government origin of the 1936 photograph, or the U.S. government authorship of the 1991 Soviet study written before the Soviet Union ended.
   - 1: For at least two documents, explains how point of view, purpose, historical situation or audience matters to the argument.
   - 0: No sourcing, or only restates authorship without explaining why it matters.
Complex understanding (0-1): Shows a complex understanding, for instance by weighing change against continuity, separating scientific understanding from political action, or using documents that qualify the main claim, such as the Soviet state causing damage or Brazil's attention to the issue fading after Eco-92.
   - 1: Corroborates, qualifies or modifies the argument with evidence, such as explaining both change and continuity or several causes of changing understanding.
   - 0: The argument stays simple or one-sided.
Note: Do not reward claims that Marsh cared only about local damage; his excerpt warns about the condition of the whole earth and the possible extinction of the human species.
Note: Muir is a voice from about 1900, not a mid-nineteenth-century observer.
Note: Arrhenius presents calculated relationships between carbon dioxide and temperature; credit students who see that the excerpt itself does not blame industry or call for policy.
Note: Document 5 can be used either as content (a steady rise of about 97 ppm from 1960 to 2020) or as sourcing (systematic government measurement as a new way of knowing).
Note: Sourcing must explain why a feature of the source matters; naming the author or date is not enough.
Note: ALTON reference — not official AP scoring

Evidence map (which documents support or complicate each line of reasoning):
- Understanding grew from damage to particular places toward the recognition that human activity could alter the whole planet, including its climate.. Supports: Document 1, 3, 5. Complicates: Document 2.
- Changing understandings were driven by visible disasters caused by economic exploitation of land, water and energy.. Supports: Document 2, 4, 6. Complicates: Document 3.
- Responsibility for understanding and responding to environmental change moved from individuals to governments, scientific institutions and international conferences.. Supports: Document 4, 5, 7. Complicates: Document 6.
- Continuity: across the whole period, observers described a lasting tension between the drive for productivity and development and long-term environmental health.. Supports: Document 1, 2, 6, 7. Complicates: Document 3.

Using the documents (use and sourcing):
- Document 1: Shows that as early as 1864 an observer argued that human 'crime' and 'improvidence' could leave the whole earth impoverished, with 'climatic excess', and could threaten the species. This is evidence that a global view of human impact existed early. Sourcing: Marsh had served as a U.S. diplomat in the Ottoman Empire and was minister to Italy, so his experience of old Mediterranean lands may help explain his long historical view of damage built up over an 'era' of human action.
- Document 2: Names specific human agents of damage in the U.S. forest reserves: lumbermen, prospectors, grazing sheep and deliberate fires. Shows conservation concern focused on protecting particular landscapes around 1900. Sourcing: As a naturalist writing a book about national parks, Muir writes as an advocate for the reserves, which shapes his harsh language about sheep as 'hoofed locusts' and about shepherds' fires.
- Document 3: Shows scientific understanding by 1906 to 1908 that small changes in atmospheric carbon dioxide could change the earth's temperature a lot, a basis for later climate concern. Sourcing: Arrhenius was a chemist writing a book on the evolution of the universe, so his purpose is scientific explanation. The excerpt presents calculations rather than a warning about human activity, which limits how far it shows concern about human impact.
- Document 4: Shows the dust storms of the 1930s on the southern Plains, a visible environmental disaster linked to farming dry grassland, and the scale of the dust compared to a single car and a fenced plain. Sourcing: The photograph was made for a U.S. government agency, the Resettlement Administration, in 1936, which shows the state recording rural environmental crisis during the Depression. As a government image, its framing reflects what the agency chose to document.
- Document 5: Shows atmospheric carbon dioxide rising steadily from about 317 ppm in 1960 to about 414 ppm in 2020, the kind of change Arrhenius had calculated could affect temperature. Sourcing: These are systematic measurements by a U.S. government scientific agency, building on Keeling's Scripps data, which shows that by the late twentieth century understanding rested on long-term institutional monitoring rather than individual observation.
- Document 6: Shows state-directed development causing severe disasters: Chernobyl, attributed to insufficient regard for safety in pursuit of energy, and the shrinking Aral Sea after rivers were diverted for cotton irrigation from 1960, plus river and air pollution. Sourcing: Written in 1991 for the U.S. government before the Soviet Union ended, the study comes out of the late Cold War. Its emphasis on Soviet 'neglect' may reflect an American government audience, though the disasters it names are well documented.
- Document 7: Shows Amazon deforestation and urban pollution drawing international attention, Brazil hosting Eco-92, a new environment ministry, and government attention fading while debate over sustainable development went on. Sourcing: A U.S. government reference work describing another country's policies, it judges Brazil's follow-through from outside. Its mention of 'unprecedented international attention' shows that environmental issues had become global diplomatic concerns.

   - "but less in basic idea than it might seem" - Defensible claim evaluating extent of change (scale and method changed, core idea and development priority continued), with a line of reasoning.
   - "The Industrial Revolution spread from Britain to the United States, Germany and Japan in the 1800s" - Describes industrialization, fossil fuels and imperial expansion and ties them to growing damage; earns the point.
   - "doubling carbon dioxide would raise the earth's temperature by about 4 degrees" - Accurate use of Docs 1-7 tied to the argument about change and continuity; earns 2.
   - "the founding of Yellowstone as the first national park in 1872" - Specific, accurate outside evidence linked to the argument about early conservation. Brief, but it counts.

   - "The government wanted to show the public how bad the crisis was so people would support its programs" - Explains the purpose of the New Deal photograph; with Marsh and Doc 6 this earns sourcing.

Sample response, middle score (4/7; Thesis/claim 1, Contextualization 0, Evidence from the documents 2, Evidence beyond the documents 0, Sourcing (point of view, purpose, situation, audience) 0, Complex understanding 1):
Understandings of how humans affect nature changed a lot between the 1860s and the early 2000s, but they did not change completely. Early writers worried about damaged land and forests, while later sources focused on the whole atmosphere and on global problems, yet people kept arguing over development versus protecting nature the whole time.

The Industrial Revolution was going on when this period started.

George Marsh in 1864 already says that the earth is becoming an unfit home because of human crime and improvidence, and he warns that people could even go extinct. So the idea that humans damage the planet was not new in the twentieth century. John Muir in 1901 writes about the forest reserves and says that they are threatened by the axe and fire of lumbermen and by sheep, which he calls hoofed locusts. His concern is more about particular forests in the United States, so it is narrower than Marsh. Then Arrhenius in 1908 uses calculations to show that if carbon dioxide doubles, the temperature of the earth's surface would rise by 4 degrees. This is a different kind of understanding because it is about the whole atmosphere and uses numbers, though the excerpt does not say that industry is causing it or that anything should be done.

Document 5 shows the carbon dioxide measurements from Mauna Loa going up from 316.91 ppm in 1960 to 414.21 ppm in 2020. This shows that the atmosphere was changing the way Arrhenius's calculations suggested it could. Document 7 about Brazil says that deforestation of the Amazon got unprecedented international attention in the late 1980s and early 1990s and that Rio hosted a UN conference in 1992. However, it also says the government's attention waned after Eco-92. This shows that even when understanding grew, action did not always follow, which supports the idea that the conflict between development and nature continued.

The Muir document was written by a naturalist who wanted the forests protected, so he has a point of view that favors conservation. Document 7 was written for the U.S. government, which is a source type that might affect what it says.

In conclusion, understanding changed from local damage to a planetary view, but Marsh already had a big view and the problems of development stayed the same, so the change was large but not total.
   - "Understandings of how humans affect nature changed a lot between the 1860s and the early 2000s, but they did not change completely." - Defensible claim about the extent of change with a line of reasoning (local damage to planetary view, but continuing development conflict). Earns the thesis point.
   - "The Industrial Revolution was going on when this period started." - Only a one-sentence passing mention of industrialization; no description of a broader development tied to the argument. No contextualization credit.
   - "Then Arrhenius in 1908 uses calculations to show that if carbon dioxide doubles, the temperature of the earth's surface would rise by 4 degrees." - Accurately describes what a document says and relates it to the topic. Together with Marsh, Muir, Document 5 and Document 7, this gives three or more documents described, earning the first evidence point. It does not use the documents to build a sustained argument, so the second point is not earned.
   - "The Muir document was written by a naturalist who wanted the forests protected, so he has a point of view that favors conservation." - Names the author's perspective but does not explain how it shapes the document or the argument. Sourcing is only stated, not explained, so no credit.
   - "This shows that even when understanding grew, action did not always follow, which supports the idea that the conflict between development and nature continued." - Gestures at continuity and the fading of Brazilian policy, but there is no developed qualification or multiple causes. This stays simple and earns no complexity credit.
   - "However, it also says the government's attention waned after Eco-92." - Uses only information from the document. There is no outside evidence such as Silent Spring, the Kyoto Protocol or the IPCC, so no evidence-beyond-documents credit.

Sample response, low score (2/7; Thesis/claim 1, Contextualization 1, Evidence from the documents 0, Evidence beyond the documents 0, Sourcing (point of view, purpose, situation, audience) 0, Complex understanding 0):
Understandings of how humans affect nature changed a great deal from the mid-nineteenth century to today, because people moved from seeing damage to local land toward seeing a problem for the whole planet, although governments kept putting economic growth first.

This change happened because of industrialization. During the nineteenth century factories, railroads and steamships spread across the world, and they ran on coal. Later the twentieth century added oil, bigger cities and huge commercial farms. As industry grew, people could change the land and the air much more than before, so more people began to worry about it, and this shaped how writers and scientists thought about nature.

Document 1 is by George P. Marsh in 1864. He says the earth is fast becoming an unfit home for people, and that this could lead to the extinction of the species. This shows that some people already thought humans were harming nature long ago. Document 3 is by Svante Arrhenius in 1908. He calculated that if carbon dioxide doubled, the temperature of the earth's surface would rise by 4 degrees. This is a scientific way of looking at the problem.

In conclusion, understandings changed a lot because the problem went from a worry about land to a worry about the whole world, but the need for growth stayed important.
   - "Understandings of how humans affect nature changed a great deal from the mid-nineteenth century to today, because people moved from seeing damage to local land toward seeing a problem for the whole planet, although governments kept putting economic growth first." - Earns the thesis point: it judges the extent of change (a great deal, with continuity in growth priorities) and sets up a line of reasoning from local damage to planetary concern.
   - "During the nineteenth century factories, railroads and steamships spread across the world, and they ran on coal." - Earns contextualization: describes industrialization and fossil fuel use and links it directly to the argument about growing human power over nature.
   - "He says the earth is fast becoming an unfit home for people, and that this could lead to the extinction of the species." - Only paraphrases Marsh and uses just two documents in total, so it does not reach the three documents needed for a point. The documents are summarized, not used to support the argument.
   - "This is a scientific way of looking at the problem." - Describes Arrhenius without using the document to support the claim about change over time. Only two documents are used, so no evidence credit.
   - "Later the twentieth century added oil, bigger cities and huge commercial farms." - General background only. No specific outside evidence such as a law, treaty, person or date is given, so no outside evidence point.
   - "Document 1 is by George P. Marsh in 1864." - Names the author and date but never explains how his position, purpose or audience shapes the document, so no sourcing credit.
   - "but the need for growth stayed important." - Mentions continuity only in passing with no evidence from the documents, so the argument stays simple and gets no complexity credit.

whap_frq.title: Changing Understandings of Human Activity and the Natural Environment, mid-19th to early 21st century

prompt.scenario: From the middle of the nineteenth century onward, industrialization, commercial agriculture, the extraction of resources and state-directed development changed landscapes, waterways and the atmosphere in many parts of the world. Writers, scientists, governments and international bodies offered different explanations of how far human activity was reshaping nature and what should be done about it. The seven documents run from George P. Marsh's 1864 book to carbon dioxide measurements taken through 2020.
prompt.task: Evaluate the extent to which understandings of the relationship between human activity and the natural environment changed from the mid-nineteenth century to the early twenty-first century.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a historically defensible thesis or claim that establishes a line of reasoning.
Describe a broader historical context relevant to the prompt.
Support an argument in response to the prompt using at least four documents.
Use at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence (beyond that found in the documents) relevant to an argument about the prompt.
For at least two documents, explain how or why the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience is relevant to an argument.
Use evidence to corroborate, qualify, or modify an argument that addresses the prompt.

sources.title: Man and Nature; or, Physical Geography as Modified by Human Action (excerpt)
sources.attribution: George P. Marsh, American diplomat and scholar, 1864 (New York: Scribner). Project Gutenberg eBook #37957. Reuse: public domain in the United States (published before 1929). excerpted (1 segment); whitespace normalized; no wording changed.
sources.context: George P. Marsh was an American diplomat who had served in the Ottoman Empire; when he published this book in 1864 he was the United States minister to Italy.
sources.body: The earth is fast becoming an unfit home for its noblest inhabitant, and another era of equal human crime and human improvidence, and of like duration with that through which traces of that crime and that improvidence extend, would reduce it to such a condition of impoverished productiveness, of shattered surface, of climatic excess, as to threaten the depravation, barbarism, and perhaps even extinction of the species.

sources.title: Our National Parks, ch. 1 (excerpt on the forest reserves)
sources.attribution: John Muir, Scottish-American naturalist, 1901 (Boston: Houghton Mifflin). Project Gutenberg eBook #60929. Reuse: public domain in the United States (published before 1929). excerpted (1 segment); whitespace normalized; no wording changed.
sources.context: John Muir was a Scottish-born American naturalist; he published this book in 1901.
sources.body: The forty million acres of these reserves are in the main unspoiled as yet, though sadly wasted and threatened on their more open margins by the axe and fire of the lumberman and prospector, and by hoofed locusts, which, like the winged ones, devour every leaf within reach, while the shepherds and owners set fires with the intention of making a blade of grass grow in the place of every tree, but with the result of killing both the grass and the trees.

sources.title: Worlds in the Making: The Evolution of the Universe (excerpt on carbonic acid and temperature)
sources.attribution: Svante Arrhenius, Swedish chemist (English translation by H. Borns), 1908 (English edition; Swedish original 1906). Project Gutenberg eBook #69022. Reuse: public domain in the United States (published before 1929). excerpted (1 segment); whitespace normalized; no wording changed.
sources.context: Svante Arrhenius was a Swedish chemist; this book was published in English in 1908.
sources.body: With the help of these data I have calculated that if the atmosphere were deprived of all its carbonic acid—of which it contains only 0.03 per cent. by volume—the temperature of the earth’s surface would fall by about 21°. This lowering of the temperature would diminish the amount of water vapor in the atmosphere, and would cause a further almost equally strong fall of temperature. The examples, so far as they go, demonstrate that comparatively unimportant variations in the composition of the air have a very great influence. If the quantity of carbonic acid in the air should sink to one-half its present percentage, the temperature would fall by about 4°; a diminution to one-quarter would reduce the temperature by 8°. On the other hand, any doubling of the percentage of carbon dioxide in the air would raise the temperature of the earth’s surface by 4°; and if the carbon dioxide were increased fourfold, the temperature would rise by 8°.

sources.title: Soviet Union: A Country Study (excerpt on environmental degradation)
sources.attribution: Raymond E. Zickel, ed., Federal Research Division, Library of Congress, 1991. Library of Congress, Federal Research Division (Country Studies; full text via Internet Archive OCR). Reuse: public domain (U.S. government work, 17 U.S.C. 105). excerpted (1 segment); whitespace normalized; OCR line-break hyphenation rejoined; running page headers/numbers removed; no wording changed.
sources.context: This reference book was written for the U.S. government in 1991, before the Soviet Union ended.
sources.body: As a consequence of this neglect, two of the twentieth century's worst man-made environmental disasters struck the Soviet Union: the Chernobyl' nuclear power plant accident, the consequence of an insufficient regard for safety to obtain increased energy; and the loss of huge amounts of water from the Aral Sea. Although the death toll from the Chernobyl' accident in 1986 was initially low, millions of people continued to live on radioactive land and raise and consume contaminated food. In addition to the human costs, cleaning up and repairing the after-effects of the accident, which continued to leak radioactive gases in 1991, were estimated to cost hundreds of billions of rubles (see Glossary) by the year 2000. The other major environmental disaster was the near destruction of the Aral Sea, whose main sources of water were diverted to irrigate arid land for the purpose of raising cotton and other crops beginning in 1960. Subsequently, the Aral Sea's coast receded sixty kilometers, in places, from its former location. Other environmental problems included the severe pollution of rivers, lakes, and the air resulting from the direct discharge of pollutants, particularly in the European part of the Soviet Union.

sources.title: Brazil: A Country Study (excerpt on deforestation and development)
sources.attribution: Rex A. Hudson, ed., Federal Research Division, Library of Congress, 1998. Library of Congress, Federal Research Division (Country Studies; full text via Internet Archive OCR). Reuse: public domain (U.S. government work, 17 U.S.C. 105). excerpted (1 segment); whitespace normalized; OCR line-break hyphenation rejoined; no wording changed.
sources.context: This reference book was written for the U.S. government; the passage describes Brazil in the early 1990s.
sources.body: The topics of rapid deforestation and extensive burning of the Amazon rain forest and environmental pollution received unprecedented international attention in the late 1980s and early 1990s. Water and air pollution had also become a serious problem for Brazil. Sao Paulo State's Tiete is so polluted that in 1992 the state was forced to launch a US$2.6 billion program to revive it. In June 1992, Rio de Janeiro hosted the United Nations (UN) Conference on the Environment and Development (Eco-92). However, the Brazilian government's attention to the problems of deforestation and pollution waned following Eco-92, despite the creation in late 1993 of the Ministry of Environment and the Amazon Region. In the mid-1990s, discussion of public policies intended to promote sustainable development (see Glossary) remained intense.

rows.name: Thesis/claim

descriptors.0: No claim, a restatement of the prompt, or a claim that does not evaluate the extent of change.
descriptors.1: Gives a defensible claim about the extent of change in understandings of human impact on nature, with a line of reasoning, in the introduction or conclusion.

rows.task_specific: A claim that evaluates how much understandings changed, for example arguing that concern moved from damaged forests, soils and regions toward a planetary and atmospheric view while the conflict between economic development and conservation continued. It must set up a line of reasoning, not just say that things changed.

rows.name: Contextualization

descriptors.0: No relevant context, or only a passing phrase.
descriptors.1: Describes a broader historical development before, during or after the period that connects directly to the argument.

rows.task_specific: Places the argument within broader developments, such as industrialization and the use of fossil fuels, imperial and commercial expansion of agriculture and resource extraction, the Great Depression and the New Deal, Cold War planned economies, or decolonization and globalization of environmental diplomacy after 1970.

rows.name: Evidence from the documents

descriptors.0: Uses fewer than three documents accurately, or only quotes or lists them.
descriptors.1: Accurately describes the content of at least three documents and relates them to the topic.
descriptors.2: Uses at least four documents to support an argument about the extent of change.

rows.task_specific: Uses what the documents actually say or show: Marsh's warning about a planet made unfit by human improvidence, Muir on grazing, logging and fire in the forest reserves, Arrhenius's calculations linking carbon dioxide to temperature, the 1936 dust storm photograph, rising Mauna Loa readings, Chernobyl and the Aral Sea, and Brazil's deforestation and Eco-92.

rows.name: Evidence beyond the documents

descriptors.0: No outside evidence, or evidence only mentioned in passing or not connected to the argument.
descriptors.1: Uses at least one specific, accurate piece of outside evidence to support the argument.

rows.task_specific: At least one specific piece of evidence not in the documents, such as the founding of Yellowstone in 1872, the Soil Conservation Service in 1935, Rachel Carson's Silent Spring in 1962, the Montreal Protocol of 1987, the creation of the IPCC in 1988 or the Kyoto Protocol of 1997, used to support the argument.

rows.name: Sourcing (point of view, purpose, situation, audience)

descriptors.0: No sourcing, or only restates authorship without explaining why it matters.
descriptors.1: For at least two documents, explains how point of view, purpose, historical situation or audience matters to the argument.

rows.task_specific: Explains how point of view, purpose, historical situation or audience shapes at least two documents, for example Marsh's diplomatic posts in the Ottoman Empire and Italy, the U.S. government origin of the 1936 photograph, or the U.S. government authorship of the 1991 Soviet study written before the Soviet Union ended.

rows.name: Complex understanding

descriptors.0: The argument stays simple or one-sided.
descriptors.1: Corroborates, qualifies or modifies the argument with evidence, such as explaining both change and continuity or several causes of changing understanding.

rows.task_specific: Shows a complex understanding, for instance by weighing change against continuity, separating scientific understanding from political action, or using documents that qualify the main claim, such as the Soviet state causing damage or Brazil's attention to the issue fading after Eco-92.

scoring_notes: Do not reward claims that Marsh cared only about local damage; his excerpt warns about the condition of the whole earth and the possible extinction of the human species.
Muir is a voice from about 1900, not a mid-nineteenth-century observer.
Arrhenius presents calculated relationships between carbon dioxide and temperature; credit students who see that the excerpt itself does not blame industry or call for policy.
Document 5 can be used either as content (a steady rise of about 97 ppm from 1960 to 2020) or as sourcing (systematic government measurement as a new way of knowing).
Sourcing must explain why a feature of the source matters; naming the author or date is not enough.
ALTON reference — not official AP scoring

defensible_theses: Understandings changed a great deal: concern with visible damage to particular forests, soils and grazing lands, voiced by individual writers such as Muir, gave way by the late twentieth century to a planetary, measured view of human impact on the atmosphere, although Marsh had already imagined human action degrading the whole earth in 1864.

Understandings changed only partly: from Marsh to the 1990s country studies, observers kept describing the same conflict between short-term productivity and long-term environmental health. What changed most was the scale of the evidence and the involvement of states and international conferences, not the basic diagnosis.

The main change was in who studied and responded to environmental damage. Concern moved from individual scholars and naturalists to government agencies, scientific monitoring networks and United Nations conferences, but state action stayed uneven, as Soviet neglect and Brazil's fading attention after Eco-92 show.
contextualization_ideas: The Industrial Revolution and the spread of coal-powered industry in the nineteenth century increased resource extraction and fossil fuel burning, which led people to question human control over nature.
The Great Depression and New Deal programs in the 1930s set the Dust Bowl inside a wider crisis of commercial agriculture and expanding state intervention in rural life.

After 1945, Cold War competition pushed rapid industrial and agricultural growth in both blocs. From the 1970s, globalization and United Nations conferences turned environmental issues into international diplomacy involving newly industrializing and postcolonial states.
outside_evidence: Yellowstone was established as the first U.S. national park in 1872.
John Muir helped found the Sierra Club in 1892.
The U.S. Soil Conservation Service was created in 1935 in response to soil erosion during the Dust Bowl.
Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962) drew public attention to the effects of pesticides such as DDT.
The Montreal Protocol (1987) set out to phase out ozone-depleting chemicals such as CFCs.
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change was established in 1988.
The Kyoto Protocol (1997) set binding greenhouse gas emission targets for industrialized countries.
Wangari Maathai founded the Green Belt Movement in Kenya in 1977 to plant trees and fight deforestation.
The 1984 gas leak at a Union Carbide pesticide plant in Bhopal, India, killed thousands of people.

doc_uses.usable_for: Shows that as early as 1864 an observer argued that human 'crime' and 'improvidence' could leave the whole earth impoverished, with 'climatic excess', and could threaten the species. This is evidence that a global view of human impact existed early.
doc_uses.sourcing: Marsh had served as a U.S. diplomat in the Ottoman Empire and was minister to Italy, so his experience of old Mediterranean lands may help explain his long historical view of damage built up over an 'era' of human action.

doc_uses.usable_for: Names specific human agents of damage in the U.S. forest reserves: lumbermen, prospectors, grazing sheep and deliberate fires. Shows conservation concern focused on protecting particular landscapes around 1900.
doc_uses.sourcing: As a naturalist writing a book about national parks, Muir writes as an advocate for the reserves, which shapes his harsh language about sheep as 'hoofed locusts' and about shepherds' fires.

doc_uses.usable_for: Shows scientific understanding by 1906 to 1908 that small changes in atmospheric carbon dioxide could change the earth's temperature a lot, a basis for later climate concern.
doc_uses.sourcing: Arrhenius was a chemist writing a book on the evolution of the universe, so his purpose is scientific explanation. The excerpt presents calculations rather than a warning about human activity, which limits how far it shows concern about human impact.

doc_uses.usable_for: Shows the dust storms of the 1930s on the southern Plains, a visible environmental disaster linked to farming dry grassland, and the scale of the dust compared to a single car and a fenced plain.
doc_uses.sourcing: The photograph was made for a U.S. government agency, the Resettlement Administration, in 1936, which shows the state recording rural environmental crisis during the Depression. As a government image, its framing reflects what the agency chose to document.

doc_uses.usable_for: Shows atmospheric carbon dioxide rising steadily from about 317 ppm in 1960 to about 414 ppm in 2020, the kind of change Arrhenius had calculated could affect temperature.
doc_uses.sourcing: These are systematic measurements by a U.S. government scientific agency, building on Keeling's Scripps data, which shows that by the late twentieth century understanding rested on long-term institutional monitoring rather than individual observation.

doc_uses.usable_for: Shows state-directed development causing severe disasters: Chernobyl, attributed to insufficient regard for safety in pursuit of energy, and the shrinking Aral Sea after rivers were diverted for cotton irrigation from 1960, plus river and air pollution.
doc_uses.sourcing: Written in 1991 for the U.S. government before the Soviet Union ended, the study comes out of the late Cold War. Its emphasis on Soviet 'neglect' may reflect an American government audience, though the disasters it names are well documented.

doc_uses.usable_for: Shows Amazon deforestation and urban pollution drawing international attention, Brazil hosting Eco-92, a new environment ministry, and government attention fading while debate over sustainable development went on.
doc_uses.sourcing: A U.S. government reference work describing another country's policies, it judges Brazil's follow-through from outside. Its mention of 'unprecedented international attention' shows that environmental issues had become global diplomatic concerns.

evidence_map.line: Understanding grew from damage to particular places toward the recognition that human activity could alter the whole planet, including its climate.
Changing understandings were driven by visible disasters caused by economic exploitation of land, water and energy.
Responsibility for understanding and responding to environmental change moved from individuals to governments, scientific institutions and international conferences.
Continuity: across the whole period, observers described a lasting tension between the drive for productivity and development and long-term environmental health.

common_pitfalls: Calling Muir a mid-nineteenth-century observer or treating Marsh as concerned only with local damage.
Claiming that Arrhenius warned against industrial emissions or called for limits; the excerpt only gives calculated relationships.
Describing details of the photograph that cannot be seen, or claiming to know the photographer's personal intentions.
Treating the country studies as neutral without considering their U.S. government origin, or treating them as primary sources from Soviet or Brazilian officials.
Summarizing documents one at a time without an argument about the extent of change.
Focusing only on the United States and ignoring the Soviet, Brazilian and global evidence.
facts: Marsh's Man and Nature was published in 1864.
Muir's Our National Parks was published in 1901.
Arrhenius's Worlds in the Making was published in Swedish in 1906 and in English in 1908; Arrhenius won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1903.
Arthur Rothstein took the Dust Bowl photograph in the Texas Panhandle in March 1936 for the Resettlement Administration.
Mauna Loa annual mean carbon dioxide rose from 316.91 ppm in 1960 to 414.21 ppm in 2020.
The Chernobyl accident occurred in 1986 in Soviet Ukraine.
The Aral Sea shrank after the Amu Darya and Syr Darya were diverted for irrigation.
The UN Conference on Environment and Development met in Rio de Janeiro in June 1992.

samples.essay:
Between the mid-1800s and the early 2000s, understandings of how humans affect nature changed a lot in scale and method, but less in basic idea than it might seem. Early writers like Marsh and Muir already believed human carelessness could ruin the land, and they judged this by looking at forests and soil. By the late twentieth century, scientists measured damage to the whole atmosphere with instruments, and governments and international meetings treated the environment as a global political issue. Still, one thing stayed the same: governments kept putting economic development ahead of protecting nature, even when they knew the risks.

This change happened because of how the world economy grew. The Industrial Revolution spread from Britain to the United States, Germany and Japan in the 1800s, and factories, railroads and steamships ran on coal. Imperial and commercial expansion also pushed farming and mining into new areas, from the American West to colonies in Africa and Asia. In the twentieth century, oil and planned economies like the Soviet Union's sped up resource use even more. So more people were seeing environmental damage, and it was getting bigger.

In the nineteenth century, concern was mostly based on what people could see. Marsh warned in 1864 that the earth was "fast becoming an unfit home" and that human "improvidence" could even lead to the "extinction of the species" (Doc 1). This shows that even early on, some thinkers saw the danger as covering the whole planet and not just one place. Marsh's point of view matters here. He was a diplomat who had served in the Ottoman Empire and Italy, places where land had been farmed and cleared for thousands of years, so he could compare old worn-out Mediterranean landscapes with the young United States and warn Americans that their land could end up like that. Muir in 1901 described logging, fires and sheep, which he called "hoofed locusts," destroying the forest reserves (Doc 2). Like Marsh he judged damage by looking at it, and he wanted it protected. This fits with the founding of Yellowstone as the first national park in 1872, which showed the U.S. government starting to set land aside.

The understanding started to shift toward the atmosphere with science. Arrhenius calculated that doubling carbon dioxide would raise the earth's temperature by about 4 degrees (Doc 3). However, his excerpt does not blame industry or ask for any policy. It is a scientific calculation, which shows that knowing about a connection did not automatically mean people saw it as a problem yet. Meanwhile, damage on the ground got worse. The 1936 photograph of a huge dust storm in the Texas Panhandle (Doc 4) shows how plowing up the Great Plains destroyed the soil. The purpose of this photo matters, because it was taken for the Resettlement Administration, a New Deal agency. The government wanted to show the public how bad the crisis was so people would support its programs to help farmers and change how land was used. This shows that by the 1930s the government itself saw human farming practices as the cause of disaster.

After 1950 the biggest change was measurement. The Mauna Loa data shows carbon dioxide rising every decade from about 317 ppm in 1960 to 414 ppm in 2020 (Doc 5). This turned Arrhenius's theory into something people could track year by year, and it gave a planetary view of human impact.

But continuity remained in how governments acted. The Soviet Union diverted rivers to grow cotton, and the Aral Sea shrank badly, and Chernobyl in 1986 came from "insufficient regard for safety" to get energy (Doc 6). This was written by the U.S. government in 1991 during the end of the Cold War, so it may have focused on Soviet failures to make communism look bad, though the disasters really did happen. Brazil also hosted Eco-92, but attention "waned" afterward (Doc 7). So even though understanding became global and scientific, the conflict between development and nature that Muir described continued into the 1990s.

samples.essay:
Understandings of how humans affect nature changed a lot between the 1860s and the early 2000s, but they did not change completely. Early writers worried about damaged land and forests, while later sources focused on the whole atmosphere and on global problems, yet people kept arguing over development versus protecting nature the whole time.

The Industrial Revolution was going on when this period started.

George Marsh in 1864 already says that the earth is becoming an unfit home because of human crime and improvidence, and he warns that people could even go extinct. So the idea that humans damage the planet was not new in the twentieth century. John Muir in 1901 writes about the forest reserves and says that they are threatened by the axe and fire of lumbermen and by sheep, which he calls hoofed locusts. His concern is more about particular forests in the United States, so it is narrower than Marsh. Then Arrhenius in 1908 uses calculations to show that if carbon dioxide doubles, the temperature of the earth's surface would rise by 4 degrees. This is a different kind of understanding because it is about the whole atmosphere and uses numbers, though the excerpt does not say that industry is causing it or that anything should be done.

Document 5 shows the carbon dioxide measurements from Mauna Loa going up from 316.91 ppm in 1960 to 414.21 ppm in 2020. This shows that the atmosphere was changing the way Arrhenius's calculations suggested it could. Document 7 about Brazil says that deforestation of the Amazon got unprecedented international attention in the late 1980s and early 1990s and that Rio hosted a UN conference in 1992. However, it also says the government's attention waned after Eco-92. This shows that even when understanding grew, action did not always follow, which supports the idea that the conflict between development and nature continued.

The Muir document was written by a naturalist who wanted the forests protected, so he has a point of view that favors conservation. Document 7 was written for the U.S. government, which is a source type that might affect what it says.

In conclusion, understanding changed from local damage to a planetary view, but Marsh already had a big view and the problems of development stayed the same, so the change was large but not total.

annotations.quote: This is a scientific way of looking at the problem.
annotations.comment: Describes Arrhenius without using the document to support the claim about change over time. Only two documents are used, so no evidence credit.

annotations.quote: Later the twentieth century added oil, bigger cities and huge commercial farms.
annotations.comment: General background only. No specific outside evidence such as a law, treaty, person or date is given, so no outside evidence point.

annotations.quote: Document 1 is by George P. Marsh in 1864.
annotations.comment: Names the author and date but never explains how his position, purpose or audience shapes the document, so no sourcing credit.

annotations.quote: but the need for growth stayed important.
annotations.comment: Mentions continuity only in passing with no evidence from the documents, so the argument stays simple and gets no complexity credit.
